name: lock-free-programming
intent: Build a shared-state algorithm whose operations are composed from indivisible atomic read-modify-write operations and a retry loop, such that the system as a whole always makes progress - no thread ever waits on another, so a preempted, stalled or crashed thread cannot prevent anyone from finishing.
problem: A mutex serialises access, and serialisation costs in three ways that get worse with scale: throughput is capped by the lock's critical section, a thread preempted or page-faulted while holding the lock stalls every other thread (convoying and priority inversion), and a thread that crashes holding the lock deadlocks the system permanently. Real systems hit exactly this - a UI thread that hangs on a lock held by a background thread doing a disk read, a trading system whose latency spikes on every GC pause inside a critical section, a kernel object whose lock is held across a context switch. Locks are fine; the point is that some components cannot afford them.
context: Applies where latency and availability must not depend on any other thread: real-time and trading systems, media and audio pipelines with hard deadlines, kernel schedulers and interrupt handlers, lock-free queues and maps under high contention, systems that must survive a thread fault, and any structure where a blocking wait would convert a slow operation into a stall. It is a discipline rather than a data structure - the queue, the stack, the map and the memory-reclamation scheme each apply it - and it requires a hardware atomic read-modify-write, a reclamation scheme for removed nodes, and a progress argument that is written down and verified.
benefits: Progress is unconditional: at least one thread always makes progress, so the system degrades in latency rather than halting. A thread that is preempted, descheduled, page-faulted or killed does not stop the others - the failure mode a mutex cannot avoid.

No lock convoying or priority inversion: there is no owner to block behind, so a low-priority thread cannot be starved by a high-priority one holding a lock, and a thread in a syscall cannot stall the pool.

Throughput scales with cores: operations on disjoint keys proceed fully in parallel, and contention produces retries (wasted work) rather than waiting (idle time) - wasted work parallelises, waiting does not.

Fault tolerance: because there is no lock to be held by a dying thread, the structure survives thread failure and arbitrary delays, which Maged and Michael's hazard-pointer results demonstrate experimentally.
Composability: non-blocking structures compose - a lock-free queue feeding a lock-free map, each with its own progress argument - and the composition preserves the system-level guarantee.

The reclamation problem gets a real answer: hazard pointers and epoch-based reclamation give lock-free memory management, which was historically the reason lock-free structures could not be used in practice.
tradeoffs: Correctness is research-grade. The algorithms rely on subtle invariants, helping protocols and precise memory orders, and the canonical implementations took years of bug reports to stabilise; hand-rolling one is not a reasonable engineering plan.

Memory reclamation is the hard part, not the queue. Removing a node from a lock-free structure while another thread is reading it is the ABA problem, and every solution (hazard pointers, epochs, RCU, a type-stable pool, a GC) has real cost in lookup, storage or memory.

Lock-freedom is not wait-freedom: an individual operation can starve indefinitely while the system progresses. Hard real-time deadlines need wait-free structures, which are much harder and usually slower.

Retries waste work. Under high contention a CAS loop can spin or fail repeatedly, so throughput collapses while CPU is saturated - a different failure shape from a lock, and one that looks like 'the CPU is busy but nothing happens'.

Cache-line contention is the actual bottleneck, not the lock: an atomic on a shared cache line ping-pongs between cores and costs far more than the instruction, so a 'lock-free' counter can be slower than a mutex that batches updates.
The algorithms are fragile under compiler and hardware change: a reordering the model does not permit, or an architecture with weaker ordering than the developer's, exposes bugs that pass every test.

Verification is expensive: correctness needs model checking or careful reasoning plus exhaustive interleaving exploration (loom, CDSChecker), because a bug in this territory reproduces once in millions of runs.
Memory ordering must be right at every access, and an over-strengthened ordering is both slower and harder to justify in review - so the code carries a burden the mutex version never had.
quality_attributes_note: Scalability and performance are the reason to pay the cost. Maintainability and simplicity are low because the algorithms are subtle and the reclamation scheme is a second, independent hard problem. Testability is low because unit tests almost never catch a memory-ordering or reclamation bug - model checking and stress testing on weak memory are the only tools that do.

participants.responsibility: The indivisible read-modify-write on which every step of every operation is built.
participants.notes: A lock-free algorithm is a sequence of these plus a retry loop; remove them and the property is gone.

participants.responsibility: Re-reads the shared state and retries when another thread won the race; the retry, not the primitive, is what makes progress.
participants.notes: Needs a pause/yield and often exponential backoff, or it livelocks under contention.

participants.responsibility: The single instant in an operation at which it takes effect; identified in the specification so the operation can be proved correct.
participants.notes: Naming it is how you check an implementation against the intended semantics.

participants.responsibility: When a thread stalls mid-operation, another thread completes it on its behalf using the descriptor it installed.
participants.notes: What turns 'a thread that might never finish' into a system that still progresses.

participants.role: Memory reclamation scheme (hazard pointers / epochs / RCU / GC)
participants.responsibility: Decides when a removed node may be freed so no thread is reading it, solving ABA as a side effect.
participants.notes: The hardest and most commonly underestimated part of a real implementation.

participants.responsibility: Resolves who wins when many threads compete, so retries do not livelock and no thread starves forever.
participants.notes: Backoff plus, in some designs, age-based priority.

participants.responsibility: The stated property of the algorithm - the system always progresses, every operation completes, or a transaction completes if left alone - which is the thing being claimed.
participants.notes: Must be written down; an unstated guarantee is not a guarantee.

use_cases: Lock-free queues and deques as the hand-off between producers and consumers where a stalled producer must not stop the consumers - Michael and Scott's algorithm is the reference implementation.
Real-time and trading pipelines with hard deadlines, where a GC pause or a thread descheduled inside a lock would exceed the deadline and latency spikes are the failure.
Kernel and operating-system data structures - scheduler run queues, slab allocators, file descriptor tables - where a thread holding a lock cannot be preempted and a fault would be unrecoverable.
Audio and media frame pipelines, where a single dropped frame is unacceptable and no thread may wait on another.
Concurrent hash maps under high write contention, where the map is the contention point and a lock around it caps throughput.
Memory allocators in multithreaded programs, where a global allocator lock is one of the most contended sites in a modern runtime.
Interrupt handlers and signal handlers sharing state with normal code, where taking a lock in interrupt context is forbidden and a lock-free flag is the only option.

Systems that must tolerate thread failure: because no lock can be held by a dying thread, the structure keeps working when a worker is killed, which the hazard-pointer experiments demonstrate explicitly.
Free-list and pool allocation for reference counting, where the decrement-and-test and the reclamation must both be non-blocking.
avoid_when: A lock works and contention is not the bottleneck - a mutex has a fast uncontended path and is vastly easier to review; lock-freedom is a solution to a problem you may not have.
The critical section is large or does I/O: lock-freedom does not help when the work itself is blocking, and a spin-wait across a syscall is pathological.
You need wait-freedom (every operation bounded) - lock-free algorithms can starve an individual thread, and meeting a hard deadline requires a wait-free design that is much harder and usually slower.
You would be writing the algorithm from scratch - use a published, reviewed implementation (Michael and Scott, Fraser, or a concurrent-collections library) rather than inventing one.

The memory reclamation problem has no acceptable answer in your environment: without a GC, hazard pointers, epochs or a type-stable pool, removed nodes cannot be safely freed and the structure is unusable.
Cache-line contention dominates anyway - if every operation touches the same word, the atomic ping-pongs and a lock with batching wins; fix the locality first.
The team cannot run model checking or stress tests on weak memory: the bugs in this territory are invisible to ordinary testing and need loom, CDSChecker or a weak-architecture target to surface.

The language or runtime gives you safe concurrent collections (Java's ConcurrentHashMap, C#'s ConcurrentDictionary, Rust's crossbeam, Go's channels) - use them; the progress guarantee is already provided and audited.
pitfalls: Ignoring memory reclamation: the queue is correct until a removed node is freed while another thread still holds a pointer to it, which is an ABA bug and a use-after-free.
Confusing lock-free with wait-free: a system can make progress overall while one thread's operation retries forever, which fails a per-operation deadline.
A retry loop with no backoff: under contention the losers spin, burning CPU and delivering no throughput, and can livelock if the winner keeps winning.
Testing only on x86: the memory-ordering bugs are invisible on a strongly-ordered architecture and appear on ARM, which is exactly where the developer's code will run in production.
Treating an atomic as a faster mutex: on a contended cache line the ping-pong can cost more than acquiring a lock, especially for a simple counter where LongAdder or per-thread batching is correct.

A missing helping protocol: if an operation can be left half-done by a stalled thread, the structure hangs until that thread returns, which is blocking in all but name - descriptors and helping are what prevent it.
Fairness omitted entirely: one thread can be starved indefinitely, which is acceptable for a cache and not for a scheduler or an allocator.
Writing the algorithm from a blog post: the published implementations have a decade of bug reports behind them and a fresh implementation has none.

related_patterns_notes.cpu-atomic-operation: The substrate. cpu-atomic-operation is one indivisible read-modify-write and its ordering contract; lock-free-programming is the multi-step method of composing them into an algorithm with a system-level progress guarantee. Neither is useful alone: the primitive has no guarantee, the method has no primitive.
related_patterns_notes.lock-free-queue: The flagship instance. The Michael-Scott queue is the canonical non-blocking structure, and its record explicitly hands memory management to hazard pointers, epochs, a type-stable pool or a GC - which is this record's hardest sub-problem.
related_patterns_notes.software-transactional-memory: Shares the technique (descriptors, helping, CAS loops) and the goal (non-blocking progress) but is a programming model for composing arbitrary operations with isolation, not a data structure. The STM literature measures the instrumentation overhead of the alternative approach explicitly.
related_patterns_notes.thread-confinement: The strongest optimisation and the one that removes the problem entirely: if no reference to the state escapes its owning thread, there is nothing to make non-blocking. Confinement beats every algorithm here.
related_patterns_notes.read-write-lock: The blocking alternative with better read throughput; it remains the right choice whenever the critical section is large or does I/O, which is most code.
related_patterns_notes.scoped-locking: RAII and defer-based lock management - the discipline this record replaces when the algorithm is non-blocking, and the correct tool everywhere else.
related_patterns_notes.double-checked-locking: Historically a broken idiom that tried to get lock-freedom on the read path with a plain field; it survives only when both the flag and the data use the acquire/release protocol this catalog's cpu-atomic-operation describes.
related_patterns_notes.object-pool: Recycling is one reclamation strategy for a non-blocking structure - reuse nodes instead of freeing them, which sidesteps ABA but bounds the pool and retains memory.
related_patterns_notes.copy-on-write: The escape from fine-grained synchronisation: if the update publishes a new immutable version with one atomic pointer store, the read path needs no atomic at all and the write path never contends with a reader.
related_patterns_notes.coroutines: A different answer to latency: cooperative coroutines eliminate blocking wait but not the contention on shared state - the non-atomic CPU work still needs the same primitives, and the event loop itself is a structured-concurrency pattern.
related_patterns_notes.intrusive-reference-counting: Reference counting is where lock-freedom is hardest and most valuable: the atomic decrement-and-test decides whether an object is destroyed, and the release ordering is what prevents a use-after-free when the count reaches zero. An intrusive reference count embedded in the object avoids a second indirection on the hot path.

anti_patterns: Using an atomic because it 'feels faster' than a lock without measuring contention - on an uncontended path the two are comparable and the lock is far easier to review.
Applying lock-free design to a counter, where LongAdder, per-thread striping or a sampled metric solves it with no atomic at all on the hot path.
Writing a CAS loop with no backoff, converting contention into a livelock that presents as 'the CPU is pegged but throughput is zero'.

Ignoring ABA because the language has a garbage collector - a GC reclaims unreachable nodes, but a node still referenced by a stalled thread can be reused by the allocator, and the ABA window is exactly there.
Claiming wait-freedom for a lock-free algorithm, then missing a deadline because one thread starved - the two properties are not interchangeable.
Testing exclusively on x86 and a single run, so memory-ordering and reclamation bugs ship to weakly-ordered hardware.
Hand-rolling a queue from a blog post instead of using a reviewed implementation that has survived years of reports.
Spinning while holding a spinlock across a syscall or an allocation, converting a non-blocking design into a system-wide stall on preemption.
design_principles: State the guarantee: lock-free, wait-free or obstruction-free is a claim about the system, and it must be written down and justified.
Non-blocking beats fast: a structure whose latency never depends on another thread is a different kind of service from a faster one that can stall.
Reclamation is part of the algorithm: ABA and use-after-free are not cleanup issues, they are correctness issues with a design.
Optimise locality before synchronisation: a cache-line ping-pong costs more than the lock it replaced, so fix the data layout first.
Measure the contention, not the primitive: the design should follow the measured contention profile, and if there is none, a mutex is the answer.
best_practices: Start from a published, reviewed implementation (Michael and Scott's queue, Fraser's work, or a mature concurrent-collections library) rather than writing an algorithm from scratch.
Verify with a model checker (loom in Rust, CDSChecker, or Relacy) - exhaustively exploring interleavings of a small protocol is the only realistic way to find the ordering bug.
Test on a weakly ordered architecture (ARM), not just x86; every memory-ordering mistake the pattern's tradeoffs describe is invisible on x86.
Add exponential backoff with a pause instruction to every retry loop and bound the retries if fairness matters.
Choose the reclamation scheme explicitly and document it - hazard pointers for reuse-heavy general structures, epochs for throughput, a GC or type-stable pool when the environment provides one.
Install a descriptor and implement helping so no operation can be left half-done by a stalled thread; that is what converts 'lock-free' from a claim into a property.
Strip the atomics to the contended minimum: batch counters, shard by thread, and prefer publishing an immutable snapshot over a fine-grained update.
Keep the progress guarantee in the type or module documentation, because the difference between lock-free and wait-free is invisible at the call site.
Bound the critical work: non-blocking progress over a large computation buys nothing - the computation still takes the same time and holds its snapshot longer.
sources: Michael and Scott, 'Simple, Fast, and Practical Non-Blocking and Blocking Concurrent Queue Algorithms' (PODC 1996) - the canonical lock-free queue, the CAS-based enqueue/dequeue, and the explicit statement that memory management is delegated to a type-preserving allocator or to hazard pointers / epoch-based reclamation. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/248052.248106

Michael and Scott, 'Fast Concurrent Queue Algorithms' (Rochester pseudocode) - the reference pseudocode and the note that the non-blocking queue requires a universal CAS or LL/SC primitive and a reclamation scheme. https://www.cs.rochester.edu/research/synchronization/pseudocode/queues.html

Maged M. Michael, 'Hazard Pointers: Safe Memory Reclamation for Lock-Free Objects' (IEEE TPDS 2004) - the lock-free reclamation method that removes the ABA problem with single-word instructions, and the experimental result that lock-free structures with hazard pointers match lock-based ones when idle and outperform them under contention. https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.1109/TPDS.2004.8

David Herlihy and Maurice Herlihy, 'Lock-Free Programming' (and the broader literature on progress guarantees) - the wait-free > lock-free > obstruction-free hierarchy, and the contention-management analysis quoted in the Clojure STM benchmarking work. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/TPDS.2004.8

Sean Kanal, 'Benchmarking Contention Management Strategies in Clojure's Software Transactional Memory Implementation' (AAU) - the explicit statement of the wait-free / lock-free / obstruction-free hierarchy and that contention management is required to avoid livelock, which is this record's fairness point. https://projekter.aau.dk/projekter/files/32587755/report.pdf

Junjie Guo / Wikipedia, 'Non-blocking algorithm' and Michael's follow-ups on lock-free memory management - the ABA problem's origin and the per-thread reference-count solution for acyclic structures. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/571825.571829
